flashcards.q: Give latency numbers for L1, L2, L3, and DRAM.
flashcards.a: L1 ~4-5 cycles (~1ns), L2 ~12-14 cycles (~3-4ns), L3 ~40-75 cycles (~10-20ns), DRAM ~200-300 cycles (~70-100ns). L1-to-DRAM ratio is roughly 100x.

flashcards.q: What is a cache line, and what size is it on x86-64/ARM64?
flashcards.a: The fixed-size unit caches move data in: 64 bytes on both x86-64 and ARM64. Touching one byte pulls the whole line into every cache level.

Two threads write to logically independent variables that happen to share a 64-byte cache line; each write invalidates the whole line for the other core per MESI, forcing repeated cross-core cache-to-cache transfers with no real data contention -- commonly 2-10x slower than padded.

flashcards.q: How do you detect false sharing in a running Linux service?
flashcards.a: perf c2c record / perf c2c report, looking for high HITM (hit-modified) counts -- the signature of cache-to-cache coherence traffic caused by (false or true) sharing.

flashcards.q: What's the correct fix for false sharing, and why is a mutex the wrong fix?
flashcards.a: Pad the contended fields to 64-byte boundaries (alignas(64), @Contended, manual padding). A mutex is wrong because there's no actual data race to synchronize -- only accidental cache-line co-location.

flashcards.q: What is a TLB miss and roughly how expensive is it?
flashcards.a: A miss in the translation lookaside buffer requiring a page-table walk (4 levels on x86-64 for 4KB pages), costing ~100+ cycles -- comparable to or worse than an L2 miss, paid in addition to the actual data access cost.

flashcards.q: How do huge pages reduce TLB pressure, and what's the operational risk of transparent huge pages?
flashcards.a: A 2MB huge page covers what would be 512 separate 4KB TLB entries, cutting miss rate for large working sets. Risk: Linux's transparent huge pages use background compaction (khugepaged) that has caused documented latency spikes (notably in Redis) -- explicit hugetlbfs avoids that.

flashcards.q: What is NUMA, and what's the typical remote-vs-local memory latency penalty?
flashcards.a: Non-Uniform Memory Access: DRAM is physically attached per-socket on multi-socket servers; a core accessing memory on another socket pays roughly 1.3-2x the local latency, with lower bandwidth, traversing the inter-socket interconnect (UPI/Infinity Fabric).

flashcards.q: List the four MESI states and what each means.
flashcards.a: Modified: sole dirty owner. Exclusive: sole clean owner, can silently upgrade to Modified with no bus traffic. Shared: multiple clean readers, a write requires invalidating all others. Invalid: stale, must refetch.

flashcards.q: What happens, state by state, when one of three cores holding a Shared cache line writes to it?
flashcards.a: The writer broadcasts an invalidation; the writer's copy goes Shared->Modified, the other two cores' copies go Shared->Invalid. Either of those cores accessing the address again is a miss requiring a cache-to-cache transfer of the Modified copy.

flashcards.q: Why is sequential array access dramatically faster than pointer-chasing a linked list of equal total size?
flashcards.a: Sequential access amortizes each 64-byte line fetch across many useful bytes and benefits from stride-based hardware prefetching. Pointer-chasing wastes most of each fetched line, is data-dependent so prefetching can't predict the next address, and each hop can be a full latency-bound miss.

flashcards.q: Design a per-CPU counter array for a highly concurrent service. What layout avoids coherence traffic?
flashcards.a: One counter per logical CPU, each padded to its own 64-byte cache line so no two CPUs' counters share a coherence unit -- each CPU writes its own line with zero cross-core invalidation; aggregation reads sum across slots, accepting eventual (not immediately exact) consistency.
